lessons.title: Fixed repetition with for and range
lessons.prepare: Python editor, paper trace grids and the loops chapter. Use whole-number donations for the example.

slides.title: Fixed repetition with for and range
slides.notes: Success means identify what repeats, list range values and trace a fixed loop. Connect Week 3 selection, which chooses a path, with iteration, which repeats a body. Introduce the three-donation task from the chapter.
body: Unit 1 · Week 4 · Lesson 1
Repeat a task a known number of times.

slides.title: Retrieval: sequence and selection
slides.notes: One minute individually, then compare explanations. Expected sequence executes instructions in order, selection chooses a branch, >= includes equality and total = total + 5 uses the old total to calculate a new total. Revisit assignment if learners interpret it as mathematical equality.
body: What does an if/else decision choose?
Why does >= include a boundary value?
Explain total = total + 5 in words.
Compare your explanation with a partner.

slides.title: What repeats in the donation task?
slides.notes: Model reading and adding one donation, then ask what should repeat for three donations. Initialise total once before repetition and display once afterwards. The loop body reads and adds. Assume suitable non-negative whole-number amounts. Use three counters or slips to act out passes before code.
body: The club records three whole-number donations.
Read one amount and add it to a running total.
Repeat those steps for each donation.
Display the final total after all three.

slides.title: range leaves out the stop value
slides.notes: Model range(3) as 0,1,2 and range(1,4) as 1,2,3. Both produce three values. Ask everyone to predict range(2,6): 2,3,4,5, then check. In these positive-step examples stop is excluded. range(0) produces no values. Python for iterates over these values and assigns each to the loop variable.

slides.title: A running total across three passes
slides.notes: Think aloud through 5,7,3: total starts 0, then becomes 5,12,15. donation_number labels passes 1,2,3. Highlight the two indented lines as the body. final print is outside the loop and displays Total: $15 once. Ask learners to point to initialisation and the repeated update. The range ends repetition after the third value.
body: Trace donations 5, 7 and 3.
Which lines repeat and which run once?
slides.code:
total = 0
for donation_number in range(1, 4):
    donation = int(input("Donation: "))
    total = total + donation
print(f"Total: ${total}")

slides.title: Prediction before paired runs
slides.notes: Driver runs the example while navigator checks the prior prediction and explains a pass, then swap roles for a second set. First set 5,7,3 gives 15; second 0,4,6 gives 10. Every learner records totals after each pass. Support: provide total-before and total-after columns. Stretch: change to four donations, predict a new input set and explain the changed range stop.
body: Write the total after each input: 5, 7, 3.
Run the program and compare with your trace.
Swap roles and predict for 0, 4, 6.
Explain how the loop knows when to finish.

slides.title: Which range gives four numbered passes?
slides.notes: Correct B: range(1,5) produces 1,2,3,4. A produces three values and C produces five values 0 through 4. Collect simultaneous responses before discussion. If several choose A, list values explicitly and recheck range(1,3). Distinguish number of passes from the final stop argument.
body: The passes must be numbered 1, 2, 3, 4.
A: range(1, 4)     B: range(1, 5)     C: range(5)
Choose alone, then list the values.
Explain why the two other choices do not fit.

slides.title: Exit ticket: explain a fixed loop
slides.notes: Expected range(2,5) gives 2,3,4 and three passes. With donations 2,4,6, running totals are 2,6,12. Initialisation stays before the loop and final output after it. Collect individual traces to identify range-stop or accumulation support for Lesson 2.
body: List the values in range(2, 5).
Trace totals for donations 2, 4 and 6.
Where should total start at zero?
Explain why the final print sits outside the loop.

lessons.title: Use a while loop to run an interactive window
lessons.prepare: Before class verify the nominated editor uses a school-approved Python/Pygame installation. Extract the whole pygame-teaching-pack.zip into a writable disposable folder. Open https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/pygame/index.html#y11-1 and workbook.md, faded_practice.py, practice-tests.csv and readiness.csv. Run python stage1_loop.py. Use supplied named state/runner infrastructure; no student-authored classes, paid media or assessed project code. Record device, interpreter and support. Paper traces support reasoning; live window/keyboard evidence remains necessary. The suggested 55-minute allocation is untrialled; use the supplied 50-minute adaptation when required.

slides.title: A loop keeps a Pygame window responsive
body: Unit 1 · Week 4 · Lesson 2
Run, trace and change the supplied window loop.
slides.notes: Open stage1_loop.py from the whole extracted teaching pack. Success: quit with both Escape and X; explain input, update, draw; predict movement and count frames. This is ungraded preparation before the project. Use primitive shapes; no assets or student classes are required. Installation/interpreter checks happen before class. Teaching lab and matching workbook: https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/pygame/index.html#y11-1; https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/pygame/workbook.md. Worked files and changed scaffold are public formative resources. Relevant Pygame references: https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/event.html ; https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/time.html ; https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/rect.html .

slides.title: Retrieve the stopping condition
body: When is a while condition checked?
What changes running from True to False?
Does counting frames measure seconds?
slides.notes: Think alone before pair comparison. A while condition is checked before each pass, so the body can run zero times. running=False ends the next loop test; it does not instantly jump out of the current body. A frame counter counts loop passes, not elapsed seconds, because frame duration varies. Retain a trace of the final failed condition. Teaching lab and matching workbook: https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/pygame/index.html#y11-1; https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/pygame/workbook.md. Worked files and changed scaffold are public formative resources. Relevant Pygame references: https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/event.html ; https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/time.html ; https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/rect.html .

slides.title: Input, update and draw repeat each frame
body: Read this excerpt inside the supplied setup.
Locate the event that changes running.
slides.notes: Run python stage1_loop.py. The complete supplied file initialises Pygame, creates the screen/clock, checks held keys, updates a bounded x and draws before flip. This seven-line excerpt focuses on X; the complete file also handles KEYDOWN Escape. Consume events every frame so the window remains responsive. Clock.tick(60) returns elapsed milliseconds and limits the target frame rate; it does not guarantee exactly 60 frames each second. Model the whole file without asking novices to recreate installation/setup code. Teaching lab and matching workbook: https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/pygame/index.html#y11-1; https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/pygame/workbook.md. Worked files and changed scaffold are public formative resources. Relevant Pygame references: https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/event.html ; https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/time.html ; https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/rect.html .

slides.title: Predict distance from elapsed time
slides.notes: The 640-pixel window and 24-pixel square give x bounds 0..616. In the supplied lab speed is 200 pixels/second: 250 ms gives 50 pixels from an interior start. For the changed speed 160: 250 ms gives 40 and 500 ms gives 80. Model first row, pairs complete the second before running. x=600 plus 40 clamps to 616, so actual change is 16. The screen origin is top-left; positive x moves right. Holding both arrows gives direction zero in the supplied expression. Teaching lab and matching workbook: https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/pygame/index.html#y11-1; https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/pygame/workbook.md. Worked files and changed scaffold are public formative resources. Relevant Pygame references: https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/event.html ; https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/time.html ; https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/rect.html .
slides.strategy: Faded worked trace and paired prediction

slides.title: Events and held keys have different jobs
body: X and Escape are discrete events.
Held arrows are checked each frame.
Read elapsed time before updating position.
slides.notes: Use the full file to contrast a KEYDOWN event with pygame.key.get_pressed(). Hold right, release, then hold left; predict x before checking. Use x = max(0, min(616, x + direction * speed * dt_ms / 1000)). This supplied clamp keeps the square inside the display. Do not add a blocking sleep. Frame count increases once per pass; time increases by each returned dt_ms. Stop a non-responsive practice script with the approved editor Stop control. Teaching lab and matching workbook: https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/pygame/index.html#y11-1; https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/pygame/workbook.md. Worked files and changed scaffold are public formative resources. Relevant Pygame references: https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/event.html ; https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/time.html ; https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/rect.html .

slides.title: Change the loop independently
body: Copy stage1_loop.py into your practice folder.
Complete movement at 160 pixels per second.
Add a frame counter and test both exit controls.
slides.notes: Fade the movement expression in a COPY; keep setup and event handling supplied. Use a separate speed variable 160 or replace the original speed constant deliberately. Predict 40 pixels at 250 ms and 80 at 500 ms from an interior position. Add frames=0 before the loop and frames+=1 inside; display/print the count without treating it as seconds. A teacher checks X and Escape on a visible desktop. At x=600, moving right for 250 ms ends at 616. If installation fails, use a labelled paper trace and record live keyboard/window evidence pending, then schedule reteaching before project issue. Teaching lab and matching workbook: https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/pygame/index.html#y11-1; https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/pygame/workbook.md. Worked files and changed scaffold are public formative resources. Relevant Pygame references: https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/event.html ; https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/time.html ; https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/rect.html .
slides.strategy: Independent changed task with optional scaffold

slides.title: Choose the correct time conversion
body: speed is pixels per second; dt_ms is milliseconds.
A: direction * speed * dt_ms
B: direction * speed * dt_ms / 1000
slides.notes: Collect simultaneous answers and reasons. B converts milliseconds to seconds. With speed 160 and dt_ms 250, A suggests 40000 pixels and B gives 40 before bounds. Do not let clamping hide the unit error: inspect an interior unbounded calculation. Revisit units if learners choose A. Teaching lab and matching workbook: https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/pygame/index.html#y11-1; https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/pygame/workbook.md. Worked files and changed scaffold are public formative resources. Relevant Pygame references: https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/event.html ; https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/time.html ; https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/rect.html .

slides.title: Show the loop working
body: Close the window using X, then Escape.
Predict movement at 250 and 500 milliseconds.
Explain a frame count and the final loop check.
slides.notes: Record expected/actual, code version and support in the y11-1 workbook/readiness row. Require a short independent explanation of input→update→draw and a changed movement test. Do not award readiness from copying the worked program. Failed exit checks trigger targeted practice before the assessed project; do not silently add project workshops. Teaching lab and matching workbook: https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/pygame/index.html#y11-1; https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/pygame/workbook.md. lessons.title: Counters, totals and loop faults
lessons.prepare: Python editor, paper trace grids and a clean three-donation program.

slides.title: Counters, totals and loop faults
slides.notes: Success means distinguish counter from accumulator, trace both and explain a repair. Use the same donation example to reduce new context while learners reason about changing state.
body: Unit 1 · Week 4 · Lesson 3
Track what changes and explain why a loop gives its result.

slides.title: Retrieval: the loop structure
slides.notes: Expected initialise before repetition, update changing state inside the body and trace the failed condition for while. A fixed known number of passes often suits for/range. Ask learners to explain how an update changes termination, then compare with notes.
body: Name something initialised before a loop.
What update can make a while condition become False?
When does a known pass count suit for/range?
Compare one explanation with a partner.

slides.title: Counting passes and accumulating values
slides.notes: Model inputs 5,7,3. count changes 0,1,2,3 while total changes 0,5,12,15. count increases by 1 per donation and total increases by the entered amount. final print displays 3 15. The name pass_number receives the values 0, 1 and 2; the separate count records completed inputs. Ask learners to mark both updates.
body: Which variable counts passes?
Which variable combines the input amounts?
slides.code:
count = 0
total = 0
for pass_number in range(3):
    donation = int(input("Donation: "))
    count = count + 1
    total = total + donation
print(count, total)

slides.title: A trace of two changing values
slides.notes: Learners complete independently: after 5 count1 total5; after 7 count2 total12; after 3 count3 total15. Ask them to compare the update rules in pairs. Support: model only the first row and provide columns. Stretch: trace a zero donation and explain why count changes even when total does not.

slides.title: A total that forgets earlier values
slides.notes: This deliberate fault resets total to zero during every pass. With 5,7,3, final total is 3. Learners predict from the intended requirement as 15, then trace the code’s actual 3, preserving the distinction. Repair by moving total = 0 before the loop. Do not change the expected result to match the faulty program.
body: Predict the final value for 5, 7 and 3.
Explain where earlier donations disappear.
slides.code:
for pass_number in range(3):
    total = 0
    donation = int(input("Donation: "))
    total = total + donation
print(total)

slides.title: A repair supported by tests
slides.notes: Learners repair reset placement and run input sets 5,7,3 ->15; 0,4,6 ->10; 0,0,0 ->0. Keep before/after traces. Ask why only testing zeros would hide the fault: both correct and faulty versions give 0. Support: show the indentation boundary. Stretch: add a counter and verify 3 even for all-zero inputs. Peer checks should challenge evidence without taking over code.
body: Move the initialisation to the correct place.
Predict and test 5,7,3 and 0,4,6.
Also test three zeros.
Explain why one passing input set is weak evidence.

slides.title: Which change affects which value?
slides.notes: If donation=0, count still increases by 1 and total stays the same. Correct B. Collect simultaneous responses, then ask learners to point to the two update expressions. If several choose A, trace an initial count0,total0 with one zero donation. Counters track events and accumulators combine values, so they need not be equal.
body: A donation is 0. What happens after that pass?
A: neither count nor total changes
B: count increases and total stays the same
Choose alone and justify from the update rules.

slides.title: Exit ticket: a trace and a repair
slides.notes: For donations 2,0,4, final count3,total6. total starts at 0 before the loop, then becomes 2,2,6. Ask learners to explain why zero input still counts as a donation. A reset inside the loop would produce final total4. Use responses to decide whether to provide the score-task skeleton next lesson.
body: Trace donations 2, 0 and 4.
State final count and total.
Explain why the zero donation still counts as a pass.
Where must total start at zero, and why?

lessons.title: A score total and mean
lessons.prepare: Python editor and a blank expected/actual log. Assume four suitable whole-number scores.

slides.title: A score total and mean
slides.notes: Success means plan and implement four inputs, accumulate their sum, calculate mean after repetition and justify tests. This is formative transfer practice from the chapter, not an extra summative assessment.
body: Unit 1 · Week 4 · Lesson 4
Build and test a program that reads four scores.

slides.title: Retrieval: what repeats and what runs once?
slides.notes: Expected input and total update repeat, total initialisation and final mean/output run once. For four passes range(4) gives 0,1,2,3. Allow individual answers before pairs discuss. Revisit accumulator placement if students put total=0 in the repeated body.
body: Which donation instructions repeated each pass?
Which instructions ran once?
List the values produced by range(4).
Explain the accumulator’s starting value.

slides.title: The score task requirements
slides.notes: Exactly four whole-number scores, suitable input assumed. The program must display sum and arithmetic mean. Learners underline four, total and mean. Use for/range because pass count is known. Choose a non-negative integer score assumption for all class tests and keep invalid text outside the core task.
body: Read exactly four whole-number scores.
Display their total and arithmetic mean.
Assume suitable non-negative scores.
Choose a loop and explain why it fits.

slides.title: Expected results before implementation
slides.notes: Calculate independently before showing answers: 8+10+6+12=36, mean36/4=9.0. For 0,0,0,0 expect total0 mean0.0. For 5,5,5,5 expect20 and5.0. Ask learners for working, not Python output. Support: add the first two scores together before the next two. Stretch: choose inputs with a non-integer mean, such as 1,2,3,5 ->11 and2.75.

slides.title: A plan with a clear loop body
slides.notes: Model the algorithm verbally, leaving Python implementation to students. Initialise total once, repeat read/add four times, then divide by four and display both results. In Python range(4) repeats four times. Explain that += is shorthand for assigning old total plus score, if learners use the chapter’s solution. Support: offer a blank loop skeleton. Stretch: explain why / preserves a fractional mean while // would discard its fraction for these non-negative inputs.
body: Set the running total to zero.
Repeat: read one score and add it, four times.
After the loop, calculate total / 4.
Display the total and mean.

slides.title: Your implementation and test record
slides.notes: Reference solution: total=0; for score_number in range(4): read score with int(input("Score: ")) then total=total+score; after the loop mean=total/4; print(total,mean). Use proper newlines and indentation. Learners run all three predicted sets, retaining expectations if actual differs. Support: provide the input line and blank loop boundaries. Stretch: use 1,2,3,5 to test a fractional mean. Ask each learner to explain a chosen line without partner help.
body: Write the program from your plan.
Run each predicted input set and record actual results.
Trace the first wrong value if a result differs.
Save your code and evidence.

slides.title: Three scores or four?
slides.notes: A loop using range(3) reads only three scores. With 8,10,6, it accumulates24, then dividing by4 gives6.0. The intended four-score result is36 and9.0. Correct the range to four passes; dividing by3 alone would still violate the four-input requirement. Collect simultaneous responses before discussion and ask learners to cite the requirement.
body: A version reads scores with range(3).
It then calculates mean = total / 4.
What requirement does it miss?
Which change fixes the input count?

slides.title: Exit ticket: defend your solution
slides.notes: For 1,2,3,5, expected total11 and mean2.75. Learners identify exactly four passes and why mean runs afterwards. Ask what their tests can and cannot establish. Check understanding of counting, accumulation and integer versus real division before Week 5 functions. Save individual work for formative follow-up.
body: Predict total and mean for 1, 2, 3 and 5.
Explain how your program reads exactly four scores.
Why calculate the final mean after the loop?
Name a test that helped you find or avoid a fault.
